title: MTH_102 — End of Semester Objective Exam

questions.q: Which condition must a rule satisfy in order to be a function?
options: Each output is produced by exactly one input
Every element of the codomain is used as an output
Each input produces exactly one output
The domain and the range contain the same number of elements
questions.why: Why C is right: a function assigns exactly one output to each input; that single-valuedness is what makes limits, gradients and areas well defined. Why the others are wrong: A states injectivity, a stronger and separate property · B states surjectivity, which concerns the codomain, not the definition · D confuses a bijection between finite sets with the definition of a function.

questions.q: A mapping sends D = {A, B, C, D} into Y = {K, 3, 9, 8, 6}. Why is it not a real-valued function?
options: The inputs are letters and not numbers
K is a possible output and is not a real number
The codomain contains more elements than the domain
Two different inputs are sent to the same output
questions.why: Why B is right: "real-valued" is a condition on the outputs, and K is not a real number. Why the others are wrong: A tests the domain, which may be any set at all · C is irrelevant, since the codomain routinely exceeds the range · D describes a non-injective function, which is still a perfectly good function.

questions.q: State the domain of f(x) = √(x − 4)/(x − 7).
questions.why: Why A is right: the root needs x − 4 ≥ 0, so x ≥ 4, and the denominator needs x ≠ 7, giving [4, 7) ∪ (7, ∞). Why the others are wrong: B wrongly excludes x = 4, where the root is 0 and the expression is defined · C checks the root and forgets the zero denominator · D reverses the root inequality to x ≤ 4.

questions.q: State the range of g(x) = (2x + 5)/(x − 3).
questions.why: Why D is right: solving y = (2x + 5)/(x − 3) for x gives x = (3y + 5)/(y − 2), valid for every y except 2 — the ratio of the leading coefficients. Why the others are wrong: A ignores the horizontal asymptote · B excludes the zero of the numerator, which is an output value, not an excluded one · C quotes the excluded domain value 3 instead of the excluded range value.

questions.q: Which of these functions has domain x > 2 rather than x ≥ 2?
questions.why: Why B is right: a root in the denominator must be strictly positive, so x − 2 > 0. Why the others are wrong: A allows x = 2, where √0 = 0 is fine · C needs only x ≥ 2, since x + 2 ≠ 0 is automatic there · D has domain [−2, 2) ∪ (2, ∞), which admits values below 2.

questions.q: If f(x) = 3x − 2 and g(x) = x² + 1, find (g ∘ f)(2).
questions.why: Why C is right: the inner function acts first — f(2) = 4, then g(4) = 17. Why the others are wrong: A is (f ∘ g)(2), the composition done in the wrong order · B multiplies f(2) by g(2) instead of composing · D drops the cross-term when expanding (3x − 2)², using 9x² + 4 in place of 9x² − 12x + 4.

questions.q: Which statement about inverse functions is correct?
options: f⁻¹(x) is another way of writing 1/f(x)
Every function defined on all of ℝ has an inverse
f and f⁻¹ always have the same domain
f has an inverse only if no two inputs share an output
questions.why: Why D is right: an inverse must send each output back to a single input, so f must be one-to-one. Why the others are wrong: A reads the −1 as a reciprocal; for f(x) = 2x + 3 the inverse is (x − 3)/2, not 1/(2x + 3) · B ignores the one-to-one requirement, which x² on ℝ fails · C swaps the rule: the domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f.

questions.q: Find f⁻¹(x) for f(x) = (3x + 1)/(x − 2).
questions.why: Why A is right: from y(x − 2) = 3x + 1 we get x(y − 3) = 2y + 1, so f⁻¹(x) = (2x + 1)/(x − 3). Checking, f(5) = 16/3 and f⁻¹(16/3) = 5. Why the others are wrong: B is the reciprocal-style flip of the fraction, not the inverse function · C keeps the right shape but flips both signs in the rearrangement · D merely negates constants in the original formula without solving for x.

questions.q: Why does x² + y² = 25 fail to define y as a function of x?
options: Its domain is not the whole of the real line
The vertical line x = 0 meets it at two points
The horizontal line y = 0 meets it at two points
Its graph is a closed curve rather than an open one
questions.why: Why B is right: at x = 0 the circle gives y = 5 and y = −5, so one input has two outputs and the vertical line test fails. Why the others are wrong: A is true but harmless — a restricted domain does not disqualify a function · C applies the horizontal line test, which tests one-to-one-ness, not functionhood · D describes the shape rather than the failing condition.

questions.q: The horizontal line test decides whether a function is:
questions.why: Why C is right: a horizontal line meeting the graph twice means two inputs sharing one output, which is exactly the failure of injectivity. Why the others are wrong: A and D name properties no line test detects at a single glance · B is decided by the vertical line test, the test students most often swap this one with.

questions.q: Which function from ℝ to ℝ is injective but not surjective?
questions.why: Why A is right: eˣ never repeats a value, so it is injective, but its outputs are only the positive reals, so it misses the negatives and is not onto ℝ. Why the others are wrong: B and D are bijections, hitting every real exactly once · C is neither, since x² repeats values and produces no negatives.

questions.q: Consider the set of pairs {(1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 3), (4, 9)}. It:
options: is not a function, because the output 3 occurs twice
is a function and is one-to-one
is not a function, because 3 appears as both input and output
is a function but is not one-to-one
questions.why: Why D is right: no input is repeated, so it is a function; but 1 and 3 both map to 3, so it is not one-to-one. Why the others are wrong: A applies the outputs-must-differ test to functionhood, which is the definition of injectivity, not of a function · B misses the repeated output · C treats an input and an output sharing a numeral as a clash, which it is not.

questions.q: In the quadratic f(x) = ax² + bx + c, the constant c is:
options: the value of the function at x = 0
the direction in which the parabola opens
questions.why: Why B is right: putting x = 0 into ax² + bx + c leaves c, so c is the y-intercept. Why the others are wrong: A is the claim the Week 2 slide itself makes wrongly; for g(x) = −2x² + 3x + 1 the vertex height is 2.125, not 1, and the two agree only when b = 0 · C is −b/(2a) · D is decided by the sign of a.

questions.q: For g(x) = −2x² + 3x + 1, find the x-coordinate of the vertex.
questions.why: Why C is right: x = −b/(2a) = −3/(−4) = 0.75. Why the others are wrong: A drops the minus sign already carried by a = −2 · B uses b/2 and forgets to divide by a · D is the vertex's y-coordinate, g(0.75) = 2.125, not its x-coordinate.

questions.q: Which description of f(x) = x⁰·⁵ and g(x) = 0.5ˣ is correct?
options: f is a power function; g is an exponential function that decays
f is an exponential function; g is a power function
Both are exponential, f growing and g decaying
f is a power function; g is an exponential function that grows
questions.why: Why A is right: x⁰·⁵ has the variable in the base, so it is a power function; 0.5ˣ has the variable in the exponent with base below 1, so it decays. Why the others are wrong: B swaps the two families entirely · C calls a power function exponential · D reads a base between 0 and 1 as growth, when only b > 1 grows.

questions.q: A function is defined by f(x) = 2x + 1 for x ≤ 0 and f(x) = x² − 3 for x > 0. Find f(−2) + f(3).
questions.why: Why D is right: −2 ≤ 0 uses 2x + 1, giving −3; 3 > 0 uses x² − 3, giving 6; the sum is 3. Why the others are wrong: A uses the x > 0 formula at x = −2, giving 1 · B uses the x ≤ 0 formula at x = 3, giving 7 · C picks the wrong branch at both points.

questions.q: The limit of f(x) as x → a exists if and only if:
options: f(a) is defined and is a real number
f is continuous at the point x = a
the left and right limits exist and are equal
the left and right limits both exist as finite numbers
questions.why: Why C is right: a limit names one destination, so the two one-sided approaches must exist and agree. Why the others are wrong: A and B confuse the limit with the function value; a limit can exist where f(a) does not · D omits the equality, which is the whole condition — a jump has both one-sided limits and no limit.

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→3) (x² − 2x − 3)/(x² − 9).
questions.why: Why B is right: substitution gives 0/0; factoring gives (x − 3)(x + 1)/[(x − 3)(x + 3)] = (x + 1)/(x + 3), which at x = 3 is 4/6 = 2/3. Why the others are wrong: A takes the ratio of the leading coefficients, a rule for limits at infinity, not at a point · C reads 0/0 as 0 · D treats 0/0 as automatic non-existence, when it is the signal to factor.

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) (√(x + 9) − 3)/x.
questions.why: Why D is right: multiplying by the conjugate turns the numerator into x, leaving 1/(√(x + 9) + 3) → 1/6. Why the others are wrong: A reads the numerator's 0 as settling the answer · B keeps only √9 = 3 in the denominator and forgets the added 3 · C mistakes 0/0 for a blow-up.

questions.q: Which approach is correct for lim(x→4) (x − 4)/(√x − 2)?
options: Rationalise, since substitution gives 0/0 and a root is present
Substitute directly, since the function is continuous at 4
Factorise and cancel, since it gives 0/0 with no root
Declare it non-existent, since the denominator tends to 0
questions.why: Why A is right: substitution gives 0/0 and a root blocks the cancellation, which is exactly the rationalisation case. Why the others are wrong: B ignores that both parts vanish at x = 4 · C would apply if there were no root; here x − 4 and √x − 2 share no polynomial factor as written · D confuses 0/0 with the k/0 form that really does blow up.

questions.q: For which limit is L'Hôpital's Rule not valid?
questions.why: Why D is right: at x = 0 this is 1/0, not indeterminate, so the rule does not apply and forcing it gives a wrong answer. Why the others are wrong: A and C are 0/0 · B is ∞/∞ · all three are the forms the rule is built for.

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) (1 − cos 2x)/x².
questions.why: Why A is right: 1 − cos 2x = 2sin²x, so the ratio is 2(sin x/x)² → 2. Two applications of L'Hôpital give the same: 2 sin 2x/2x, then 4 cos 2x/2 = 2. Why the others are wrong: B is the answer to the different limit (1 − cos x)/x² · C stops at the first 0/0 and reads it as zero · D stops one step early, reporting 4 cos 2x without dividing by the 2 from the denominator.

questions.q: Given lim(x→a) f(x) = 4 and lim(x→a) g(x) = −2, evaluate lim(x→a) [3f(x) − g(x)²].
questions.why: Why C is right: the power and constant-multiple laws give 3(4) − (−2)² = 12 − 4 = 8. Why the others are wrong: A squares −2 and keeps the minus sign, getting 12 + 4 · B applies the 3 to the whole bracket, computing 3(4 − 4) · D drops the g² term entirely.

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) x² cos(1/x).
options: It does not exist, because cos(1/x) oscillates
questions.why: Why B is right: cos(1/x) stays between −1 and 1, so −x² ≤ x²cos(1/x) ≤ x², and both bounds tend to 0; the squeeze theorem forces the limit to 0. Why the others are wrong: A treats cos(1/x) as tending to cos 0 = 1, but 1/x runs to infinity, not to 0 · C is right that cos(1/x) has no limit but forgets that x² crushes the oscillation · D confuses a bounded oscillation with a blow-up.

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→∞) (4x³ + 2x)/(3x³ − x²).
questions.why: Why C is right: the degrees are equal, so the limit is the ratio of the leading coefficients, 4/3. Why the others are wrong: A applies the rule for a denominator of higher degree · B applies the rule for a numerator of higher degree · D takes the numerator's leading coefficient alone and treats the denominator's as 1.

questions.q: Which of the following is not one of the three conditions for continuity at c?
options: f must be differentiable at c
questions.why: Why A is right: differentiability is a stronger condition than continuity and forms no part of its definition — |x| is continuous at 0 and not differentiable there. Why the others are wrong: B, C and D are precisely the three conditions quoted in Week 4, so none of them can be the odd one out.

questions.q: A graph shows the left branch rising to height 3 at x = 2 and ending in an open circle, a filled dot at (2, 1), and the right branch starting from an open circle at height −4. Which reading is correct?
options: Left limit 3, right limit −4, limit 1, f(2) = 1
Left limit 3, right limit −4, limit does not exist, f(2) = 1
Left limit 3, right limit −4, limit does not exist, f(2) undefined
Left limit 3, right limit −4, limit 1, f(2) undefined
questions.why: Why B is right: the one-sided limits are 3 and −4, which differ, so the limit does not exist; the filled dot gives f(2) = 1. Three separate questions, three separate answers. Why the others are wrong: A and D let the function value decide the limit, which it never does · C reads the filled dot as an open circle and declares f(2) undefined.

questions.q: Let f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3) for x ≠ 3 and f(3) = k. For what k is f continuous at x = 3?
questions.why: Why D is right: for x ≠ 3 the function simplifies to x + 3, so the limit is 6, and continuity forces f(3) = 6. Why the others are wrong: A leaves the hole unfilled · B substitutes the point x = 3 rather than the limit value · C evaluates the original numerator x² at 3 instead of the simplified expression.

questions.q: Classify the discontinuities of f(x) = (x² − 16)/(x² − 3x − 4).
options: Removable at x = 4; infinite at x = −1
Infinite at x = 4 and at x = −1
Infinite at x = 4; removable at x = −1
Jump at x = 4; infinite at x = −1
questions.why: Why A is right: factoring gives (x − 4)(x + 4)/[(x − 4)(x + 1)]. At x = 4 the factor cancels and the limit is 8/5, so the discontinuity is removable; at x = −1 nothing cancels and the numerator is −15, so the function blows up. Why the others are wrong: B assumes every zero of the denominator is an asymptote, skipping the factorisation · C reverses the two points · D calls a hole a jump, though a jump needs two different finite one-sided limits.

questions.q: A discontinuity can be removed by redefining the function at a single point when:
options: the graph has a break of finite size there
the function runs to infinity on one side
both one-sided limits exist and are equal there
the function oscillates without settling there
questions.why: Why C is right: if both one-sided limits exist and agree, redefining f at that point to equal the common value satisfies all three continuity conditions. Why the others are wrong: A is a jump, which one point cannot bridge · B is an infinite discontinuity, where no finite value works · D is the oscillating essential case, where no one-sided limit exists at all.

questions.q: For f(x) = 1/(x − 3), the point x = 3 is:
options: a removable discontinuity, since the denominator cancels
an infinite discontinuity, with a vertical asymptote there
a jump discontinuity, since the two sides go opposite ways
no discontinuity at all, since 3 is outside the domain
questions.why: Why B is right: the factor x − 3 does not cancel, the numerator is 1 there, so the function runs to ±∞ and x = 3 is a vertical asymptote. Why the others are wrong: A invents a cancellation that is not available · C mistakes opposite infinite behaviour for a finite jump; a jump needs two finite limits · D treats "outside the domain" as meaning "no discontinuity", but every discontinuity of this kind sits outside the domain.

questions.q: Let f(x) = x² for x < 2 and f(x) = 3x − 4 for x ≥ 2. At x = 2, f has:
options: no discontinuity, since both pieces are polynomials
a removable discontinuity at the point (2, 4)
a jump discontinuity, the left limit being 4 and the right 2
an infinite discontinuity, the two pieces running apart
questions.why: Why C is right: the left limit is 2² = 4, the right limit is 3(2) − 4 = 2, both finite and unequal, so the graph breaks by a fixed amount. Why the others are wrong: A assumes polynomial pieces guarantee continuity, ignoring the join · B would need the two one-sided limits to agree · D would need the function to run to infinity, which no polynomial piece does at a finite point.

questions.q: Which statement is true?
options: If lim(x→c) f(x) exists then f is continuous at c
If f(c) is defined then lim(x→c) f(x) exists
If f is continuous at c then f(c) equals the left limit only
If f is continuous at c then lim(x→c) f(x) exists
questions.why: Why D is right: continuity at c requires the limit to exist as its second condition, so continuity implies existence. Why the others are wrong: A reverses the implication; a hole has a limit and no continuity · B also reverses it; f(c) can be defined at a jump where no limit exists · C invents a one-sided version of the definition — continuity forces agreement with both sides.

questions.q: Geometrically, the derivative of f at a point is:
options: the slope of the tangent to the curve at that point
the slope of the chord joining two points on the curve
the area between the curve and the x-axis up to that point
the average rate of change over an interval
questions.why: Why A is right: sliding the second point of a chord into the first pivots the line until it touches at one point, and the derivative is that tangent's gradient. Why the others are wrong: B is the average rate of change, the quantity before the limit is taken · C describes the integral, not the derivative · D is again the chord gradient, correct only over an interval.

questions.q: Differentiate f(x) = 2x² + 3x from first principles.
questions.why: Why D is right: f(x + h) − f(x) = 4xh + 2h² + 3h; dividing by h gives 4x + 2h + 3, and letting h → 0 leaves 4x + 3. Why the others are wrong: A drops the derivative of 3x · B comes from expanding (x + h)² as x² + h², which loses the 2xh cross-term and hence the whole 4x · C applies the power rule as though the coefficient 2 did not multiply the 2x.

questions.q: Why can the derivative of a product not be u′v′?
options: Because u′v′ is undefined when either derivative is zero
Because applying it to x·x would give 1 instead of 2x
Because the product rule must always produce a quotient
Because u and v may have different domains
questions.why: Why B is right: x·x = x² has derivative 2x, while u′v′ would give 1·1 = 1. The correct rule u′v + uv′ gives 1·x + x·1 = 2x. Why the others are wrong: A invents a definedness problem that does not exist · C confuses the product rule with the quotient rule · D raises a domain issue irrelevant to the algebra.

questions.q: Differentiate y = 5x³ − 6/x² + 4√x.
questions.why: Why A is right: rewriting as 5x³ − 6x⁻² + 4x^(1/2) gives 15x² + 12x⁻³ + 2x^(−1/2). Why the others are wrong: B keeps the minus sign, forgetting that differentiating x⁻² produces −2x⁻³ which cancels against the existing minus · C multiplies rather than reduces the fractional power, turning 4x^(1/2) into 8√x · D reduces the negative power to x⁻¹ instead of x⁻³ and leaves the root undifferentiated.

questions.q: Differentiate y = (3x − 2)(x² + 4).
questions.why: Why C is right: with u = 3x − 2 and v = x² + 4, the rule gives 3(x² + 4) + (3x − 2)(2x) = 9x² − 4x + 12. Expanding first confirms it. Why the others are wrong: A uses u′v′ · B loses the sign on −2(2x) = −4x · D takes only u′v plus v′, omitting the u factor in the second term.

questions.q: Differentiate y = (2x + 3)/(x² + 1).
questions.why: Why B is right: the numerator is 2(x² + 1) − (2x + 3)(2x) = −2x² − 6x + 2, over (x² + 1)². Why the others are wrong: A reverses the numerator to uv′ − u′v, which flips every sign · C forgets to square the denominator · D differentiates numerator and denominator separately, which is L'Hôpital's Rule misapplied as a derivative rule.

questions.q: Differentiate y = (2x³ − 5)⁴.
questions.why: Why D is right: the chain rule gives 4(2x³ − 5)³ times the inner derivative 6x², that is 24x²(2x³ − 5)³. Why the others are wrong: A omits the inner derivative, the single commonest chain-rule error · B omits the outer coefficient 4 · C multiplies correctly but never reduces the power from 4 to 3.

questions.q: For the circle x² + y² = 25, find the gradient of the tangent at (3, 4).
questions.why: Why C is right: differentiating implicitly, 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y = −3/4 at (3, 4). Why the others are wrong: A loses the minus sign that the rearrangement produces · B and D invert the ratio, giving the gradient of the normal rather than the tangent (and B also keeps the sign).

questions.q: For f(x, y) = x³y² + 4x − 7y, find ∂f/∂y.
questions.why: Why A is right: holding x constant, x³y² differentiates to 2x³y, 4x contributes 0, and −7y contributes −7. Why the others are wrong: B is ∂f/∂x with the −7 wrongly carried; differentiating with respect to the wrong variable · C treats the frozen 4x as if it were 4x differentiated to 4 · D differentiates x and y at once in the first term, which defeats the purpose of a partial derivative.

questions.q: When differentiating implicitly, why does y³ give 3y²(dy/dx) rather than 3y²?
options: Because y³ is a product and needs the product rule
Because y is a function of x, so the chain rule applies
Because implicit equations always carry an extra dy/dx factor
Because the derivative of y with respect to y is dy/dx
questions.why: Why B is right: y stands for an unwritten function of x, so y³ is a composite and the chain rule contributes the factor dy/dx. Why the others are wrong: A calls a power a product · C states the symptom as though it were a rule, with no reason attached · D is a real confusion: dy/dy is 1, and the extra factor comes from the chain rule, not from that.

questions.q: Given x = t² + 1 and y = t³ − 3t, find dy/dx at t = 2.
questions.why: Why D is right: dx/dt = 2t = 4 and dy/dt = 3t² − 3 = 9, so dy/dx = 9/4. Why the others are wrong: A divides the wrong way round; dy belongs on top to match dy/dx · B forgets to divide by dx/dt at all · C uses (d²y/dt²)/(d²x/dt²) = 6t/2, which is not the second derivative and certainly not the first.

questions.q: The third derivative of position with respect to time is called:
questions.why: Why A is right: differentiating position three times gives jerk, the rate at which acceleration changes — the term the Week 6 summary uses. Why the others are wrong: B is the second derivative · C is the first · D is mass times velocity, not a derivative of position at all.

questions.q: For y = x⁵ − 3x⁴ + 2x² − 7, find y‴.
questions.why: Why C is right: y′ = 5x⁴ − 12x³ + 4x, y″ = 20x³ − 36x² + 4, y‴ = 60x² − 72x. Why the others are wrong: A stops at the second derivative · B carries the constant 4 through a differentiation, though constants go to zero · D goes one round too far to y⁽⁴⁾.

questions.q: Which statement about d²y/dx² and (dy/dx)² is correct?
options: They are equal for every differentiable function
They are equal whenever the function is a polynomial
Both name the second derivative in different notation
They differ: for y = x² they are 4x² and 2
questions.why: Why D is right: they are unrelated. For y = x², (dy/dx)² = (2x)² = 4x², while d²y/dx² = 2. Why the others are wrong: A and B claim an equality that a single example destroys · C treats the two symbols as notation for one thing, which is the misreading the question targets.

questions.q: At a stationary point where f″(a) < 0, the function has:
options: a curve that is concave up
questions.why: Why B is right: f″ < 0 means the curve is concave down, so a stationary point there sits at the top of a cap. Why the others are wrong: A would require f″ = 0 with a change of sign · C is the f″ > 0 case · D reverses the meaning of the sign of f″.

questions.q: A particle moves so that s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t. Find its acceleration at t = 1.
questions.why: Why C is right: v(t) = 3t² − 12t + 9 and a(t) = 6t − 12, so a(1) = −6. Why the others are wrong: A is v(1), the velocity rather than the acceleration · B drops the minus sign from 6 − 12 · D is s(1), the position, one differentiation short twice over.

questions.q: For a polynomial of degree 6, which derivative is the first that is identically zero?
questions.why: Why A is right: each differentiation drops the degree by one, so the sixth derivative is a non-zero constant and the seventh is the first identically zero one. Why the others are wrong: B is the constant derivative, not the zero one — the classic off-by-one · C still contains an x term · D is zero but is not the first such derivative.

questions.q: The second derivative of a function measures:
options: the slope of the tangent to the curve
the total area under the first derivative
the rate at which the curve crosses the axis
the concavity, or how the slope changes
questions.why: Why D is right: the second derivative is the rate of change of the slope, which is concavity — the basis of the second-derivative test. Why the others are wrong: A is the first derivative · B reverses the operation, describing integration of f′ · C describes roots, which no derivative measures.

questions.q: Why must an indefinite integral carry the constant + C?
options: Because the integral sign is not considered well-formed without it
Because differentiation destroys constants, so antiderivatives form a family
Because area under a curve is measured from an arbitrary starting point
Because the limits of integration have not yet been supplied here
questions.why: Why B is right: x³, x³ + 7 and x³ − 500 all differentiate to 3x², so running backwards recovers a whole family and + C names it. Why the others are wrong: A treats the constant as notation rather than mathematics · C describes definite integrals and a choice of reference point · D is nearly right in spirit but wrong in fact — a definite integral has limits and still needs no + C.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫x⁻¹dx.
questions.why: Why A is right: n = −1 is the one exponent the power rule cannot handle, and its antiderivative is ln|x| + C, with the bars covering negative x. Why the others are wrong: B applies the power rule anyway and divides by zero · C differentiates instead of integrating · D integrates x⁻¹ as though it were x⁻³ or similar.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫(6x² − 4x + 3)dx.
questions.why: Why C is right: term by term, 6x³/3 = 2x³, −4x²/2 = −2x², and 3x, plus C. Why the others are wrong: A differentiates rather than integrates · B forgets to divide the middle term by 2 · D has the right antiderivative but omits + C, which loses a mark every time.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫(4/x³ + 3√x)dx.
questions.why: Why B is right: 4x⁻³ integrates to 4x⁻²/(−2) = −2/x², and 3x^(1/2) to 3x^(3/2)/(3/2) = 2x^(3/2). Why the others are wrong: A multiplies by 3/2 instead of dividing by it · C loses the minus sign generated by dividing by −2 · D divides by 3 instead of by −2 in the first term.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫ from 1 to 3 of (3x² − 2x)dx.
questions.why: Why D is right: F(x) = x³ − x², so F(3) − F(1) = 18 − 0 = 18. Why the others are wrong: A computes F(1) − F(3), reversing the Fundamental Theorem · B substitutes into the integrand rather than the antiderivative, getting 21 − 1 · C writes + C on a definite integral, where it cancels and must not appear.

questions.q: The integral ∫ from 0 to 2 of (x² − 4)dx comes out negative. This means:
options: the region lies below the x-axis on that interval
the antiderivative was found with a sign error
the limits were written in the wrong order
the area of the region is −16/3 square units
questions.why: Why A is right: on [0, 2] the parabola x² − 4 lies below the axis, so the strips count negatively and the signed integral is −16/3. Why the others are wrong: B blames the algebra when the answer is correct · C would flip the sign but the limits are in order · D calls a signed integral an area; the area is 16/3 and areas are never negative.

questions.q: Which statement about definite integrals is false?
options: ∫ from a to a of f(x)dx = 0
Interchanging the limits reverses the sign
A definite integral is always positive
∫ from a to b plus ∫ from b to c equals ∫ from a to c
questions.why: Why C is right: this is the false statement — a definite integral is signed, and ∫ from 0 to 2 of (x² − 4)dx is negative. Why the others are wrong: A, B and D are all standard true properties, so choosing any of them means missing the signed nature of the integral.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to π/2 of cos x dx.
questions.why: Why D is right: the antiderivative of cos x is sin x, so the value is sin(π/2) − sin 0 = 1 − 0 = 1. Why the others are wrong: A evaluates sin(π/2) as 0, confusing it with sin π · B uses −sin x as the antiderivative, importing the minus sign that belongs to ∫sin x dx · C integrates cos x as though it were 1, giving the interval length.

questions.q: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus states that ∫ from a to b of f(x)dx equals:
options: F(b) − F(a) + C, where F′ = f
questions.why: Why B is right: with F any antiderivative of f, the integral equals F(b) − F(a); the arbitrary constant cancels in the subtraction. Why the others are wrong: A substitutes into f rather than F · C reverses the order of subtraction · D adds a constant that has already cancelled and must never be written on a definite integral.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫3x²(x³ + 2)⁴dx.
questions.why: Why A is right: with u = x³ + 2 we have du = 3x²dx, exactly the factor present, so the integral becomes ∫u⁴du = u⁵/5. Why the others are wrong: B divides by 3 as well, double-counting the 3x² already absorbed into du · C forgets to divide by the new power 5 · D leaves an x factor outside, meaning the substitution was never completed.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫x/(x² + 4)dx.
questions.why: Why C is right: u = x² + 4 gives du = 2x dx, so x dx = du/2 and the integral is (1/2)ln(x² + 4) + C. Why the others are wrong: A forgets the 1/2 from converting x dx into du/2 · B invents a product rule for integration, which does not exist · D is the answer to ∫dx/(x² + 4), where there is no x in the numerator to absorb.

questions.q: For ∫x ln x dx, the LIATE guideline gives:
options: u = x, dv = ln x dx
u = ln x, dv = x dx
u = x ln x, dv = dx
u = 1, dv = x ln x dx
questions.why: Why B is right: LIATE puts Logarithmic before Algebraic, so u = ln x, which simplifies to 1/x on differentiation, and dv = x dx integrates easily. Why the others are wrong: A reverses LIATE and forces you to integrate ln x, the harder half · C leaves the whole integrand as u, which changes nothing · D takes u = 1 so that du = 0 and the formula collapses uselessly.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫x e^(3x)dx.
questions.why: Why D is right: u = x, dv = e^(3x)dx gives v = e^(3x)/3, so the result is xe^(3x)/3 − ∫e^(3x)/3 dx = xe^(3x)/3 − e^(3x)/9 + C. Why the others are wrong: A drops the minus sign that stands before the second integral in the formula · B integrates e^(3x)/3 without dividing by 3 again · C omits the division by k = 3 in both places.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫ln x dx.
questions.why: Why C is right: treating the integrand as ln x times 1, parts with u = ln x and dv = dx gives x ln x − ∫x(1/x)dx = x ln x − x + C. Differentiating returns ln x. Why the others are wrong: A differentiates instead of integrating · B loses the minus sign in uv − ∫v du · D applies a power rule to a logarithm, which the standard forms do not support.

questions.q: Which substitution suits ∫dx/√(x² − 16)?
questions.why: Why A is right: the pattern √(x² − a²) with a = 4 calls for x = a sec θ, since sec²θ − 1 = tan²θ collapses the root. Why the others are wrong: B suits √(a² − x²), a difference with the variable second · C suits √(a² + x²), a sum · D uses a = 16 when the constant under the root is 16 = 4², so a is 4.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫dx/√(25 − x²).
questions.why: Why B is right: this is the arcsin standard form with a = 5, giving arcsin(x/5) + C. Differentiating confirms the 1/5 from the chain rule cancels against the 5 pulled out of the root. Why the others are wrong: A is the arctan form, which belongs to 1/(a² + x²), a sum with no root · C uses 25 in place of a = 5 · D inserts a spurious 1/5; the constant already cancels.

questions.q: Writing (5x − 4)/[(x − 2)(x + 1)] as A/(x − 2) + B/(x + 1), find A and B.
questions.why: Why D is right: from 5x − 4 = A(x + 1) + B(x − 2), setting x = 2 gives 6 = 3A so A = 2, and x = −1 gives −9 = −3B so B = 3. Checking at x = 0 gives −4 on both sides. Why the others are wrong: A pairs each constant with the wrong factor · B mishandles the double negative in −9 = −3B · C also flips the sign of A by substituting into the wrong bracket.

questions.q: Before splitting (x³ + 1)/(x² − 4) into partial fractions you must first:
options: divide, since the numerator has higher degree
rationalise the denominator using its conjugate
substitute u = x² − 4, since du = 2x dx appears
complete the square in the denominator first
questions.why: Why A is right: the numerator has degree 3 and the denominator degree 2, so long division must come first; splitting straight away produces an inconsistent system. Why the others are wrong: B rationalises where there is no root · C substitutes where du = 2x dx is not present · D completes the square, which is for irreducible quadratics; x² − 4 factorises cleanly.

questions.q: Which statement about integrating a product is correct?
options: The integral of a product equals the product of the integrals
Every product is integrated by partial fractions
No product rule exists; the technique depends on the integrand
The differentiation product rule reverses directly into an integral rule
questions.why: Why C is right: as the Week 8 introduction says, integration has no systematic rule set matching differentiation's; substitution, parts, trigonometric substitution or partial fractions must be chosen to suit the integrand. Why the others are wrong: A asserts the false identity ∫fg = (∫f)(∫g) · B applies one technique universally, though partial fractions need a factorisable rational function · D claims the product rule reverses into a formula, when reversing it actually yields integration by parts, a different statement.

questions.q: An integral is improper when:
options: the integrand contains a square root of a variable
a limit is infinite, or the integrand blows up on it
the antiderivative is not an elementary function
the integral evaluates to a negative number
questions.why: Why B is right: an integral is improper when a limit is infinite (Type I) or the integrand has an infinite discontinuity on the interval (Type II). Why the others are wrong: A confuses a root with a singularity · C is about elementary antiderivatives, which is a separate difficulty · D mistakes a negative value for impropriety.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫ from 1 to ∞ of dx/x³.
questions.why: Why D is right: lim(t→∞)[−1/(2x²)] from 1 to t = 0 + 1/2 = 1/2. Here p = 3 > 1, so it converges. Why the others are wrong: A misreads the p-test; only p ≤ 1 diverges on [1, ∞) · B is the value of ∫ from 1 to ∞ of dx/x², the neighbouring case · C uses the exponent 3 as the answer instead of computing x^(−2)/(−2).

questions.q: The integral ∫ from 1 to ∞ of dx/x:
questions.why: Why C is right: the antiderivative is ln x, and ln t → ∞, so the integral diverges. This is the p = 1 boundary case. Why the others are wrong: A confuses it with ∫ from 1 to ∞ of dx/x², which does converge to 1 · B and D substitute the lower limit ln 1 = 0 and ignore the unbounded upper end.

questions.q: The integral ∫ from 0 to 1 of dx/xᵖ converges when:
questions.why: Why A is right: near 0 the problem is the spike, so the integrand must blow up slowly; that requires a small exponent, p < 1. Why the others are wrong: B is the condition for the other row of the p-test, on [1, ∞) — the two rows are opposites and are constantly swapped · C and D put the boundary case p = 1 on the convergent side, though it diverges in both rows.

questions.q: Which of these converges?
questions.why: Why D is right: on [1, ∞) convergence needs p > 1, and 3/2 > 1. Why the others are wrong: A has p = 1/2 ≤ 1 on an infinite interval, so it diverges · B has p = 2 ≥ 1 near zero, so it diverges · C has p = 3/2 ≥ 1 near zero, which diverges — the same exponent that converges in D, which is exactly why the two rows must be kept apart.

questions.q: Suppose 0 ≤ f(x) ≤ g(x) for all x ≥ a. Then:
questions.why: Why B is right: f's region sits inside g's, so a finite area for the larger forces a finite area for the smaller. Why the others are wrong: A reverses the direction; the smaller converging says nothing about the larger · C likewise reverses it; the larger diverging says nothing about the smaller · D mixes convergence and divergence into a conclusion the test never yields.

questions.q: To show ∫ from 1 to ∞ of e^(−x²)dx converges, compare it with:
options: e^(−x) from below, since e^(−x) ≤ e^(−x²) for x ≥ 1
1/x, whose integral is known to diverge
e^(−x) from above, since e^(−x²) ≤ e^(−x) for x ≥ 1
e^(x²), whose integral is known to diverge
questions.why: Why C is right: for x ≥ 1 we have x² ≥ x, so −x² ≤ −x and e^(−x²) ≤ e^(−x); since ∫ from 1 to ∞ of e^(−x)dx = 1/e converges, the smaller integral converges too. Why the others are wrong: A states the inequality backwards, and bounding below by a convergent integral proves nothing · B compares with a divergent integral, and a divergent upper bound gives no conclusion · D compares with a function that grows rather than decays, so the inequality runs the wrong way.

questions.q: The integral ∫ from 0 to 1 of dx/√x:
options: diverges, since the integrand is undefined at 0
questions.why: Why A is right: this is Type II, improper at 0, and lim(t→0⁺)[2√x] from t to 1 = 2 − 0 = 2. Why the others are wrong: B assumes an improper integral must diverge, when the whole point is that some converge · C forgets the factor 2 in the antiderivative 2√x · D divides by 2 instead of multiplying, integrating x^(−1/2) as if the new power were −1/2 again.

questions.q: The Riemann sum Σf(x)Δx becomes the integral ∫f(x)dx because:
options: the strips are added rather than multiplied
as the strip width tends to zero the sum reaches a limit
the antiderivative of a sum is the sum of the antiderivatives
each strip has area f(x) rather than f(x)Δx
questions.why: Why B is right: each strip has area f(x)Δx; summing and letting Δx → 0 turns Σ into ∫ and Δx into dx. The notation records the limit. Why the others are wrong: A describes an operation, not a limit · C states linearity, which is a separate property · D misstates the strip area, dropping the width that makes it an area at all.

questions.q: Find the total area between y = x² − 9, the x-axis, x = 0 and x = 4.
questions.why: Why D is right: the curve crosses at x = 3, so split. On [0, 3] the integral is 9 − 27 = −18, giving area 18; on [3, 4] it is 64/3 − 36 + 18 = 10/3. The total is 18 + 10/3 = 64/3. Why the others are wrong: A integrates straight through, giving the signed value −44/3 · B takes the magnitude of that signed value, which is still not the area · C keeps only the first piece.

questions.q: Find the area enclosed between y = x² and y = x + 6.
questions.why: Why C is right: x² = x + 6 gives x = −2 and x = 3, with the line on top; ∫ from −2 to 3 of (x + 6 − x²)dx = 13.5 − (−7.333) = 125/6. Why the others are wrong: A evaluates the antiderivative at x = 3 only and forgets to subtract the value at x = −2 · B loses a factor from the cubic term · D subtracts bottom from top the wrong way round, giving a negative "area".

questions.q: Find the total area between y = x³ and y = x from x = −1 to x = 1.
questions.why: Why A is right: the curves cross at −1, 0 and 1, so the top curve swaps. Each half contributes 1/4, giving 1/2. Why the others are wrong: B integrates x − x³ straight through, and the odd symmetry cancels the halves to give the net value 0 · C uses one half only · D doubles the wrong quantity.

questions.q: Before finding the area bounded by y = f(x) and the x-axis on [a, b], you must check:
options: whether f is differentiable on [a, b]
whether a is smaller than b
whether f attains a maximum on [a, b]
whether f crosses the x-axis inside [a, b]
questions.why: Why D is right: if the curve crosses the axis inside the interval, the pieces have opposite signs and must be split before their magnitudes are added. Why the others are wrong: A asks for a condition integration does not need · B is a formality that changes the sign, not the method · C concerns extrema, which play no part in an area calculation.

questions.q: The formula ∫[f(x) − g(x)]dx still gives the area when both curves lie below the x-axis, because:
options: areas are defined as absolute values in every case
the strip height f(x) − g(x) stays positive either way
the integral of a negative function is always positive
two negative areas cancel to leave a positive one
questions.why: Why B is right: the strip runs from the lower curve to the upper one, so its height is f(x) − g(x), and the subtraction cancels whatever shared negative part the two curves have. Why the others are wrong: A appeals to absolute values, but the formula itself has none · C is simply false — integrating a negative function gives a negative number · D describes cancellation that would leave nothing, not the area.

questions.q: Find the area enclosed between y = 4 − x² and the x-axis.
questions.why: Why A is right: the curve meets the axis at x = ±2, and ∫ from −2 to 2 of (4 − x²)dx = [4x − x³/3] = 16 − 16/3 = 32/3. Why the others are wrong: B integrates over [0, 2] only, giving half the symmetric region · C drops the x³/3 term altogether · D keeps only the x³/3 contribution.

questions.q: For y = x³ on the interval [−2, 2], the definite integral and the total area are respectively:
questions.why: Why C is right: x³ is odd, so the signed integral over the symmetric interval is 0; the area is twice ∫ from 0 to 2 of x³dx = 2(4) = 8. Why the others are wrong: A reports the signed value as the area, ignoring the piece below the axis · B reports the area as the integral, ignoring the cancellation · D swaps the two answers.

questions.q: Revolving y = f(x) about the x-axis, the disc method gives:
questions.why: Why D is right: a slice at x is a disc of radius f(x) and thickness dx, of volume π[f(x)]²dx. Why the others are wrong: A forgets to square the radius, the commonest single error in this topic · B carries the shell method's 2π and still no square · C squares correctly but drops the π, so the answer is not a volume of discs at all.

questions.q: The region under y = √x from x = 0 to x = 9 is revolved about the x-axis. Find the volume.
questions.why: Why B is right: V = π∫ from 0 to 9 of (√x)²dx = π∫x dx = π[x²/2] = 81π/2. Why the others are wrong: A omits the division by 2 from integrating x · C forgets to square, integrating √x to give 18π · D uses the upper limit 9 without squaring it in the antiderivative.

questions.q: The region between y = x² and y = 2x is revolved about the x-axis. Find the volume.
questions.why: Why C is right: the curves meet at x = 0 and 2, with 2x outside and x² inside, so V = π∫ from 0 to 2 of (4x² − x⁴)dx = π(32/3 − 32/5) = 64π/15. Why the others are wrong: A squares the difference of the radii, π∫(2x − x²)²dx = 16π/15, the defining error of the washer method · B halves the correct value, as if only one radius mattered · D uses 5 rather than 15 as the common denominator.

questions.q: Revolving about the y-axis, the shell method gives:
options: V = 2π∫ from a to b of x·f(x)dx
V = π∫ from a to b of x·f(x)dx
V = 2π∫ from a to b of f(x)dx
V = 2π∫ from a to b of [f(x)]²dx
questions.why: Why A is right: unrolling a shell gives a sheet of height f(x), length 2πx and thickness dx, so V = 2π∫x f(x)dx. Why the others are wrong: B drops the factor 2, halving every answer · C drops the radius x, which is the whole point of the method · D imports the disc method's square into a shell formula.

questions.q: The region bounded by y = x², the x-axis and x = 3 is revolved about the y-axis. Find the volume.
questions.why: Why B is right: V = 2π∫ from 0 to 3 of x·x²dx = 2π[x⁴/4] = 2π(81/4) = 81π/2. Why the others are wrong: A uses π rather than 2π · C drops the x radius factor, integrating x² alone · D applies the disc formula π∫[f(x)]²dx in x, which revolves about the wrong axis.

questions.q: The washer formula subtracts the squares of the radii rather than the radii themselves because:
options: the outer radius always exceeds the inner radius
subtracting the radii would always give a negative result
a washer's area is πR² − πr², and (R − r)² is not R² − r²
questions.why: Why D is right: the washer's cross-sectional area is πR² − πr², and expanding (R − r)² gives R² − 2Rr + r², a different quantity entirely. Why the others are wrong: A is a labelling convention, not a reason · B confuses positivity with correctness — the wrong formula is positive too · C is false, since R > r makes R − r positive.

questions.q: Revolving y = √(r² − x²) from x = −r to x = r about the x-axis gives:
questions.why: Why C is right: V = π∫ from −r to r of (r² − x²)dx = π[r²x − x³/3] = π(2r³ − 2r³/3) = 4πr³/3, the known volume of a sphere. Why the others are wrong: A is an area formula, with the wrong dimensions for a volume · B is the value before doubling across the symmetric interval · D drops the factor 4/3 that the x³/3 term produces.

questions.q: A region is described in terms of x and revolved about the y-axis, and f cannot easily be inverted. The natural method is:
questions.why: Why A is right: shells about the y-axis integrate in x, so no inversion of f is needed — that is exactly the situation the method exists for. Why the others are wrong: B revolves about the wrong axis · C and D both integrate in y, which requires writing x as a function of y, the very step the question says cannot easily be done.

questions.q: The organising principle behind every application in this part of the course is:
options: differentiate a total to obtain a rate
integrate a rate to obtain a total
differentiate a rate to obtain an acceleration
multiply a rate by the length of the interval
questions.why: Why B is right: velocity to distance, marginal cost to total cost, discharge rate to total discharged — every application in Week 12 integrates a rate over an interval to get a total. Why the others are wrong: A runs the process backwards, which is differentiation · C describes going one step further down the derivative chain · D would be correct only for a constant rate, and the point of these problems is that the rate varies.

questions.q: A particle has velocity v(t) = 3t² − 12 m/s. Find the distance it travels in the first 3 seconds.
questions.why: Why D is right: v changes sign at t = 2, so split: |−16| + 7 = 23 m. Why the others are wrong: A is the magnitude of the displacement, which is not the distance when the particle reverses · B is the displacement itself, and distances are never negative · C keeps only the first leg.

questions.q: A spring has constant k = 250 N/m. Find the work done stretching it 0.4 m from its natural length.
questions.why: Why A is right: with a varying force, W = ∫ from 0 to 0.4 of 250x dx = 125(0.16) = 20 J. Why the others are wrong: B multiplies the final force 100 N by the distance 0.4 m, treating a varying force as constant · C reports the final force kx = 100 in joules · D halves the correct answer once too often.

questions.q: Marginal cost is MC(x) = 3x² − 4x + 20 naira per unit and fixed costs are ₦500. Find the total cost of producing 10 units.
questions.why: Why C is right: C(x) = x³ − 2x² + 20x + 500, since the fixed cost is the constant of integration; C(10) = 1000 − 200 + 200 + 500 = ₦1500. Why the others are wrong: A sets the constant to zero and loses the fixed cost · B doubles the fixed cost or adds it twice · D evaluates the marginal cost MC(10) = 280 instead of the total cost.

questions.q: A factory discharges a pollutant at r(t) = 100e^(0.05t) kg per day. Find the total discharged in the first 10 days.
questions.why: Why D is right: ∫ from 0 to 10 of 100e^(0.05t)dt = [2000e^(0.05t)] = 2000(e^(0.5) − 1) ≈ 1297 kg. Why the others are wrong: A multiplies the initial rate 100 by 10 days, treating a growing rate as constant · B gives the rate on day 10, 100e^(0.5) ≈ 164.9 kg per day, not a total · C forgets to divide by k = 0.05, so the answer is 20 times too small.

questions.q: Demand is given by p = 60 − 3q and the market settles at q = 15. Find the consumer surplus.
questions.why: Why B is right: p* = 60 − 45 = 15, ∫ from 0 to 15 of (60 − 3q)dq = 562.5, and subtracting the ₦225 actually paid leaves ₦337.50. Why the others are wrong: A stops at the integral and never subtracts what buyers paid · C is the amount paid, p*q*, not the surplus · D adds the two quantities instead of subtracting.
